title: The Boom Before the Bust
hook: The sales board glows green while the first skipped log sheet curls beside the vat.
counterintuition: The danger is not success itself. It is letting strong results certify habits that will break the group when conditions change.
tryThisNow: Pick one practice currently praised because results are good and ask what behavior it is training if pressure changes.
keyTakeaway: A boom should be read for hidden costs and trained habits before success makes the habits feel too valuable to question.

breakdown.fastRead:
A record month can hide the first skipped temperature log. A sold-out season can hide unpaid cleanup and unsafe crowd flow. Success is not proof that the system is healthy. It may only prove that the system has not yet met the condition that exposes its weakness.

The boom before the bust is a warning about trained habits. When results are strong, leaders stop diagnosing. They protect the shortcut because the numbers look good. The better move is to ask what the boom is teaching people to repeat.
breakdown.deepRead:
A boom gives leaders cover. Orders rise, seats sell, grants arrive, waitlists grow, demos impress. The room feels rewarded, and the practices attached to that reward gain authority. A skipped log becomes practical. An oversized class becomes efficient. Weekend builds become commitment. Delayed service becomes smart use of cash.

This is how hidden cost gets trained. People do not have to be greedy for it to happen. They learn from what the room praises and what it ignores. If record sales get applause while the temperature log disappears, the lesson is clear. If sellouts get celebrated while cleanup becomes unpaid and invisible, the culture is learning whose cost does not count. Strong results postpone diagnosis because the evidence everyone sees looks like success.

Success can train the failure that follows it.

The leadership move is to audit the boom while it still feels good. Which habit did this result reward? Which cost was hidden because the number was strong? Which exception would become dangerous if repeated for six months? This is not an anti-success stance. It is how you keep success from becoming proof that no one is allowed to ask harder questions.
breakdown.fullRead:
A bust rarely appears from nowhere. Often the bust is built during the boom, one praised exception at a time. The organization learns that the shortcut is maturity, the delay is discipline, the extra load is loyalty, and the missing check is harmless because the month ended well. By the time conditions change, the habits have become part of identity.

You can see it in small businesses and public work long before it reaches any grand economic scale. A creamery grows orders and treats the missing culture-temperature log as the price of speed. A venue sells out and treats unpaid cleanup as part of the magic. A tree nursery wins a grant and counts photo-op plantings while saplings die after care is gone. A studio earns praise for prototype velocity and quietly trains crunch as normal. None of these scenes is simply greed. Each is success teaching the group what it can get away with.

Ask one question during the good month: what would this habit do to us if the cushion disappeared?

That question changes the diagnosis. The leader can honor the result while refusing to worship the method. Yes, the season sold out. Which sellouts required staff to work past the plan? Yes, enrollment is full. Which speaking turns disappeared when the room got too large? Yes, the tourist surge lifted revenue. Which engine-service tags got postponed until the ferry's busy months were doing the maintenance budget's work?

The limit matters. Not every boom contains rot. Sometimes success reflects real quality, timing, and effort. Leaders should not treat good news as suspicious by default. The point is narrower: success is not enough evidence to stop inspecting the habits attached to it. Good results tell you something worked. They do not tell you whether the system can keep working without hidden debt.

A mature leader therefore studies success with the same discipline used for failure. What did we reward? What did we ignore? What cost was displaced? What behavior will people copy next time because it received recognition from above? If the answer points to care, quality, and trust, the boom may be strengthening the culture. If it points to skipped checks, hidden fatigue, and deferred repair, the bust is already being rehearsed.

The hardest moment to question a habit is when it is winning. That is why the work has to happen then. Once the bust arrives, everyone can see the failure mechanism. Leadership is seeing it while the room is still clapping.

examples.title: Nora Finds the Missing Log

planSpec.stakes: growth rewards shortcuts that later spoil batches
planSpec.requiredBeat: she compares the record sales month with the first skipped culture-temperature log

examples.scenario: A copper vat shines beside a missing temperature log as Nora reviews the month that set the creamery record. The first spoiled batch arrived later, but the habit began earlier. She compares the record sales week with the first blank culture-temperature line and sees which shortcut success had taught everyone to protect. For this regional cheese creamery expansion case, Nora is the manager close enough to act.
examples.whatToDo: Match the record sales month to the first skipped temperature log, then restore the log as a non-negotiable production step before accepting more orders.
examples.whyItMatters: Nora does not blame growth itself. She identifies the habit the boom rewarded before the spoiled batches make the cost obvious.

examples.title: Malcolm Marks the Cleanup Cost

planSpec.stakes: success hides staff exhaustion and unsafe crowd patterns
planSpec.requiredBeat: the promoter marks which sellouts required unpaid cleanup before booking the next run

examples.scenario: "We should add four more nights," the agent says while Malcolm looks at a ticket manifest under a barrier diagram. Every show sold out, but two nights needed unpaid cleanup and one crowd lane jammed near the bar. Malcolm is about to decide whether sellout status proves the model or whether the next run must price the hidden cost. In the concert venue booking office, Malcolm is the lead responsible for the next handoff.
examples.whatToDo: Mark each sellout that required unpaid cleanup or unsafe crowd flow before booking more dates. Build staffing and barriers into the next offer.
examples.whyItMatters: Malcolm questions the method without dismissing success. The strong season should not make exhaustion and crowd risk untouchable.

examples.title: Celine Slows the Grant Calendar

planSpec.stakes: fast planting numbers mask poor survival care
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director slows the next planting after matching last year's photo op dates to dead saplings

examples.scenario: A tree tag scratches against a brittle sapling in the nursery wind. Celine holds the grant calendar that made last year's planting count look perfect. The photos were on time, but many saplings died before summer. Before signing the next schedule, she must decide whether funding rewards speed or survival.
examples.whatToDo: Match photo-op dates to dead saplings, slow the next planting schedule, and add survival checks before public count updates.
examples.whyItMatters: Celine reads the boom for the habit it trained. The grant should reward living trees, not a fast number that hides care failure.

examples.title: Irene Caps the Roster

planSpec.requiredBeat: she watches a teacher skip speaking turns and caps enrollment before complaints arrive

examples.scenario: Irene celebrated the waitlist until she stood beside a classroom door with placement cards stacked in her hand. The class roster was full, and the teacher skipped three speaking turns to finish the lesson. Before complaints arrived, Irene capped enrollment and protected practice time from the boom.
examples.whatToDo: Watch a full class, count missed speaking turns, and cap enrollment before the waitlist defines quality. Let learning time set the limit.
examples.whyItMatters: The waitlist was a good sign, but it was training oversized groups. Irene protects the promise that made the school attractive.

examples.title: Jasper Circles the Weekend Notes

planSpec.stakes: demo success trains crunch as normal
planSpec.requiredBeat: the producer circles the weekend build notes and asks which habit will break at launch

examples.scenario: What breaks at launch if this is how we win the demo? Jasper asks, tapping the build number on the whiteboard. The bug list is shorter than expected because two artists worked Sunday. "That is commitment," someone says. Jasper circles the weekend build notes and must decide whether praise is training crunch as normal.
examples.whatToDo: Circle the weekend build notes, name the demo success, and ask which habit would break at launch scale. Reset the sprint rule before praise hardens it.
examples.whyItMatters: Jasper keeps velocity from becoming a cultural debt. The demo worked, but the method may be teaching a failure mechanism.

examples.title: Noa Links Sales to Service Tags

planSpec.requiredBeat: the operator ties each record-sales week to the postponed engine-service tags

examples.scenario: You stand with Noa by an engine-room valve while a service tag hangs behind the cafe's sales ledger. The tourist surge made every week look smart. Noa ties each record-sales week to a postponed service tag and sees that the busy months had been borrowing trust from the ferry's maintenance plan.
examples.whatToDo: Pair record-sales weeks with postponed service tags, then reserve maintenance time before adding cafe hours. Make the ledger show the cost it hid.
examples.whyItMatters: Noa does not treat the surge as bad. She stops busy revenue from certifying maintenance deferral as wisdom.

questions.prompt: A bakery's new wholesale account doubles revenue, and the team starts skipping cooling checks to fill orders. No complaints have arrived yet. What should the owner ask first?
choices: How fast can we add more accounts?
Who is least excited about growth?
What habit is this boom teaching before spoilage exposes it?
questions.explanation: The first question reads success for trained habits. More accounts may deepen the shortcut, and excitement level misses the hidden cost.

questions.prompt: A clinic clears a record number of appointments by shortening intake questions. Patient ratings remain high for now. Which diagnosis best fits the boom-before-bust lens?
choices: High ratings prove the shorter intake is safe.
The strong result may be training a shortcut whose cost appears later.
The clinic should avoid high appointment numbers.
questions.explanation: Good results do not prove the method is healthy. The point is not anti-volume, but early diagnosis of hidden cost.

questions.prompt: A venue sells out every weekend but relies on unpaid cleanup after midnight. The promoter wants to expand. Which action best questions success without dismissing it?
choices: Cancel future shows because sellouts are suspicious.
Ignore cleanup because fans love the venue.
Price cleanup and crowd control into the next run before adding dates.
questions.explanation: The correct action honors demand while surfacing hidden cost. Canceling is overreaction, and ignoring cleanup lets success protect exploitation.

questions.prompt: A startup is praised for shipping prototypes quickly because everyone works weekends. The product is not yet failing. What is the leadership risk?
choices: Weekend work always proves people care.
Fast prototypes should never be celebrated.
The praise may train crunch as the normal path to success.
questions.explanation: The praised habit may become a future failure mechanism. Celebration is not the problem; unexamined method is.

questions.prompt: A grant-funded program wins praise for planting thousands of trees, but survival checks show many died after photo events. Which metric should guide the next cycle?
choices: Photo-op count alone because it secures funding.
Total trees ordered regardless of care capacity.
Survival after planting, tied to care staffing and schedule.
questions.explanation: Survival connects success to purpose. Photo counts and order totals reward visible boom while hiding the care failure.

questions.prompt: A manager says, "Why question our process when results are the best we've had?" Which answer best preserves the lesson?
choices: Good results are useful evidence, but they do not reveal every hidden cost or trained habit.
Good results should always be distrusted.
Process questions should wait until failure occurs.
questions.explanation: The answer respects results while keeping diagnosis open. Waiting for failure lets the habit become harder to change.

questions.prompt: A language school has full waitlists, but teachers skip speaking turns to fit everyone in. What should the owner do before complaints appear?
choices: Cap classes based on speaking turns and protect practice time.
Raise prices and keep adding students.
Tell teachers to speak faster.
questions.explanation: The cap ties success to the school's purpose. More students or faster teachers may worsen the habit the boom is training.

questions.prompt: A ferry cafe has record tourist sales while engine-service tags keep getting postponed. What hidden-cost question should the operator ask?
choices: Which maintenance debt did each record week require?
How can we make the cafe busier next month?
Why does the engine room resist revenue?
questions.explanation: The question links visible success to hidden cost. The other choices either chase more or frame maintenance as obstruction.

questions.prompt: A director faces a live decision. A leader wants to know whether a boom is strengthening or weakening culture. Which evidence is most useful?
choices: Whether recognition from above goes to habits that protect care, quality, and trust.
Whether the numbers are larger than last year.
Whether critics of the boom sound negative.
questions.explanation: The recognition pattern shows what success is training. Bigger numbers alone cannot reveal hidden costs, and tone-policing critics avoids diagnosis.

reviewCards.front: A practice is praised because results are strong. What should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask what behavior the boom is training and what hidden cost would appear if pressure changed or the cushion vanished.
Visible results make the method feel proven. Leaders may stop inspecting skipped checks, hidden fatigue, or displaced cost.

reviewCards.front: How do you question a boom without becoming anti-success?
reviewCards.back: Honor the result, then inspect the method. Ask which habits made the result and whether those habits can be repeated safely.

reviewCards.front: What is recognition from above teaching during a boom?
reviewCards.back: It teaches which behaviors are worth copying. If recognition ignores hidden cost, people will repeat the shortcuts that produced the number.

reviewCards.front: When is the best time to inspect a winning habit?
reviewCards.back: During the good month, before the habit becomes identity and before the bust makes the failure obvious.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice studying success as carefully as failure. Strong results deserve credit, but they also deserve a hidden-cost audit before the method becomes untouchable.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a team hits a record result, then I will ask which checks, rest, or repair steps were skipped to get there.
If leadership praises a result, then I will name the habit being rewarded and whether we want that habit repeated.
If success creates pressure to expand, then I will price hidden labor, quality risk, and maintenance before approving more.
If someone questions a winning practice, then I will treat the question as diagnosis rather than disloyalty.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one recent win and write two columns: the visible result and the hidden habit it may be training.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one successful process for skipped checks, deferred repair, hidden labor, or quality drift.

memorableLines.text: Success can train the failure that follows it.
memorableLines.why: It states the core warning sharply.

memorableLines.text: The hardest moment to question a habit is when it is winning.
memorableLines.why: It names why leaders miss the boom's risk.

memorableLines.text: The boom before the bust is a warning about trained habits.
memorableLines.why: It frames the chapter's practical audit.
